How We Cut Our CI Pipeline From 40 Minutes to 6

Contents

  1. The problem: a 40-minute wall
  2. Step one: measure everything
  3. Test sharding with historical timing data
  4. Remote build and test caching
  5. Killing flaky tests for good
  6. Results and what we would do differently

The problem: a 40-minute wall

Every engineer at Northwind knew the ritual. You open a pull request, write a careful description, request review, and then you wait. And wait. Our CI pipeline had crept upward for three years until the median wall-clock time to a green checkmark reached forty minutes and eleven seconds. Developers had learned to context-switch away mid-review, and our pull requests sat open for an average of fourteen hours before first review. The pipeline was not just slow; it was quietly reshaping how the entire organization worked.

We set a hard target at the start of the quarter: median pipeline under ten minutes, p95 under fifteen, without cutting coverage below the 82% gate. This post is the full story of how we got to six minutes median — what worked, what was a waste of effort, and the surprising cultural problems that surfaced along the way.

Step one: measure everything

Before touching a single configuration file, we spent two weeks building a pipeline telemetry dashboard. Every job emitted a structured timing event: queue delay, environment setup, dependency restore, compile, test execution, artifact upload, and teardown. Within a week we had thirty thousand pipeline runs instrumented, and the data overturned several assumptions.

The compile phase, which everyone assumed was the bottleneck, took a median of only four minutes. The real monster was test execution: twenty-two minutes at the median, with a long tail of JavaScript integration suites that each spun up their own containerized Postgres. Worse, queue delay averaged nine minutes during peak hours because our runners were provisioned for a concurrent load profile from 2023.

The lesson: instrument before you optimize. We would have wasted a quarter caching compiles when the actual problem was test scheduling and queue capacity.

Test sharding with historical timing data

Our monorepo held roughly 14,000 test cases across Jest, pytest, and Go test. The original CI config split tests into eight shards by directory, which balanced file count but not execution time. One shard always drew the payment integration suite and ran eleven minutes longer than the others.

We replaced directory sharding with timing-weighted sharding. Each test case reports its duration to our telemetry pipeline, and the sharder packs shards greedily, longest first, targeting a per-shard budget of four minutes. The implementation is about two hundred lines of Python and reads a parquet file of timing history that the CI system refreshes after every main-branch run.

def shard(tests, budget_s=240.0, shards=8):
    ordered = sorted(tests, key=lambda t: -t.p50_duration)
    groups = [[] for _ in range(shards)]
    totals = [0.0] * shards
    for t in ordered:
        i = min(range(shards), key=lambda k: totals[k])
        groups[i].append(t)
        totals[i] += t.p50_duration
    return groups

The first run of the new sharder cut test execution from twenty-two minutes to seven and a half. The greedy packing isn't optimal, but it is deterministic and easy to debug, which mattered more to us than squeezing out the final percentage point that an exact solver would provide.

Handling newly added tests

New test cases have no timing history. We solved this pragmatically: unobserved tests get a conservative default estimate of the p75 duration for their test type, and their first real timing sample corrects the estimate on the next run. This meant the shard balance degraded gracefully on branches that added many tests rather than falling off a cliff.

Remote build and test caching

With execution balanced, the next target was redundant work. Every pull request rebuilt compiler artifacts and re-ran tests for code paths the changes could not possibly reach. We introduced a content-addressed remote cache keyed on the transitive input hash of each build target.

Dependency compilation hit rates were excellent from day one: 94% of pull-request builds restored their full toolchain and third-party dependencies from cache. Test result caching was harder. We only cache test results for targets whose transitive closure of source files is unchanged, which required generating a precise dependency graph. For our Go services we used the native build list; for TypeScript we wrote a tsconfig-paths aware graph builder; for Python we gave up on precise graphs and rely on sharding alone.

If you are evaluating this approach, budget real time for cache eviction policy. We initially kept entries for thirty days and filled a two-terabyte bucket in eleven days. We now keep main-branch artifacts for thirty days and branch artifacts for four, which holds steady at about 600 GB.

Killing flaky tests for good

A six-minute pipeline is worthless if 8% of runs fail spuriously. Our flake rate at the start of the quarter was 7.9%, which meant nearly every developer hit a red build that "just needs a retry" every week. Retries masked the problem and added minutes of hidden latency.

We ran a four-week flake elimination push with three policies:

  1. Automatic quarantine. Any test that fails and then passes on the same commit without a code change is quarantined within the hour. Quarantined tests run on a nightly schedule and post a daily digest.
  2. Root-cause review, not retry review. Every quarantined test gets an owner and a two-week deadline. The owning team either fixes the test, fixes the product bug it exposed, or deletes the test with a documented rationale.
  3. No new time-based assertions. Tests that assert elapsed time, animation frames, or debounce windows must use virtual clocks. The linter rejects real-clock sleeps in test code.

The flake rate fell from 7.9% to 0.4% in six weeks. Roughly a third of quarantined tests turned out to be exposing genuine race conditions in the product — including a session-token refresh bug that had been silently logging out about forty users a day.

Flaky tests are not a testing problem. They are nondeterminism leaking out of your system, and the pipeline is just the first place anyone notices.

— Priya Raghavan

What did not work

Two investments underdelivered. First, moving the largest integration suites to a container-native runner saved only forty seconds per suite once sharding existed; the migration cost two engineer-weeks. Second, an experiment with ML-based test selection predicted skipped tests with good precision but the engineering cost of maintaining feature flags around every skip was unsupportable. We shelved both after measuring them honestly.

Results and what we would do differently

The final numbers, measured across the four weeks following full rollout:

Pipeline performance before and after optimization
MetricBeforeAfter
Median wall-clock40m 11s6m 02s
p95 wall-clock63m 40s11m 18s
Median queue delay9m 05s11s
Flake rate7.9%0.4%
Median time to first review14.2 hours3.1 hours

The review-latency improvement was the payoff nobody predicted. When feedback arrives in minutes, authors stay in context, reviewers triage while the change is fresh, and stacks of dependent pull requests merge the same day.

If we started over, we would do measurement first (we did), sharding second (we did), and skip the container-runner migration entirely until the last possible moment. The unglamorous truth is that balanced scheduling and honest flake triage delivered 80% of the win, and everything else was polish.

Want to dig into the sharder? It is open source under northwind/ci-sharder, and the telemetry schema is documented in our pipeline telemetry docs. For background on why slow feedback loops compound, we recommend the research summary in ACM Queue and the DORA research program findings on deployment frequency.
